How to price a home inspection: a full worked example

Say you're quoting a 2,800 sq ft, two-story house on a crawlspace foundation, built 45 years ago. The buyer wants a same-day report, and they've asked for a radon test and a sewer scope on top of the standard inspection. Here is every line item, computed by the calculator at $95/hr, a 30-mile round trip at $0.70/mile, a 15% rush premium, $35 overhead, and a 25% target margin.

StepAmount
Base on-site time (2,800 sq ft) + 2nd story (+0.25 hr) + crawlspace (+0.5 hr) + 45-year age band (+0.5 hr)4.75 hrs
Labor cost (4.75 hrs × $95/hr)$451.25
Rush premium (15% of labor, not travel or add-ons)$67.69
Travel (30 miles × $0.70/mile)$21.00
Radon test$150.00
Sewer scope$175.00
Overhead$35.00
Total cost$899.94
Suggested fee (cost ÷ (1 − 25% margin))$1,199.92
Profit$299.98

Compare that to the same house with no rush, no add-ons, and a slab foundation instead of a crawlspace — the shape most flat per-square-foot fee schedules would still price close to identically, because they only look at the 2,800 sq ft number:

ChangeEffect
Slab instead of crawlspace−0.5 hr on-site (−$47.50 labor before margin)
No rush reportNo rush premium at all, versus $67.69 above
No radon or sewer scope−$325.00 in add-on fees

A flat "$0.20 per square foot" rule would quote both houses the same $560 and either overprice the easy one or, more often, underprice the crawlspace-and-add-ons job by several hundred dollars — money that has already been spent by the time the report goes out.

Five bookings a week at this job's $299.98 profit clears $1,499.90 toward a weekly income goal — short of a $2,000 target by $500.10, or two more inspections at the same margin. That's what the calculator's weekly income check is for: not just "is this one job priced right," but "does a full week of these actually clear what I need to earn."

Common questions

How much should I charge for a 2,800 sq ft home inspection with a crawlspace?

Using this calculator's model at $95/hr, a 30-mile round trip at $0.70/mile, a same-day rush premium, radon and sewer-scope add-ons, $35 overhead, and a 25% target margin, the suggested fee is $1,199.92 — see the full breakdown above for every line item.

Why is the crawlspace and age premium added in hours instead of dollars?

Because the cost driver is time on site, and your hourly rate converts that to dollars consistently whatever your rate happens to be. Adding a flat dollar premium instead would either overcharge an inspector with a lower rate or undercharge one with a higher rate for the same extra half hour of crawling.

Should I always charge the same fee for the same square footage?

No. Two houses of the same square footage can take very different amounts of time depending on stories, foundation access, and age-related wear. Pricing by square footage alone is the flat-rate shortcut this calculator exists to avoid; the worked example above shows two houses that would price identically under a flat per-square-foot rule but differ by hundreds of dollars once stories, foundation, age, rush, and add-ons are accounted for.

FOR INDEPENDENT HOME INSPECTORS

Price the inspection before you've even seen the crawlspace.

A franchise brand hands its inspectors a fee schedule. Independents build their own, and the number that actually drives on-site time — stories, foundation access, the home's age — is easy to fold into a flat per-square-foot guess that quietly underprices an older crawlspace house. This free calculator prices one inspection from those specifics, adds radon, sewer scope, termite/WDO, and mold at their own fee, and checks whether a week of bookings hits your income goal.

See a full worked example in how to price a home inspection.

Common questions

Why does a crawlspace or basement cost more than a slab foundation?

A slab has nothing underneath to inspect. A crawlspace means suiting up and physically moving through a tight space to check the underside of the structure, and a basement usually holds the mechanicals (furnace, water heater, panel) in one place that still has to be inspected on top of the rest of the house. This calculator adds a flat time premium for each, on top of the square-footage base.

Why does the rush report premium apply to labor time and not to travel or add-ons?

A same-day or rush turnaround costs you scheduling flexibility on the inspection itself, not a discount on the mileage you already drove or the radon canister you already paid for. This calculator applies the rush premium to on-site labor cost only, the same way an after-hours premium applies to billed time rather than to parts in this portfolio's other trade calculators.

Why are radon, sewer scope, termite/WDO, and mold priced as flat add-on fees instead of more minutes?

Each of those is usually a separate instrument, a separate specialist visit, or a lab sample with its own turnaround — not simply more time spent walking the same house. Pricing them as their own flat fee keeps that cost visible instead of folding it into a vaguer per-square-foot number.

Does this calculator replace my own state licensing requirements or InterNACHI/ASHI Standards of Practice?

No. It only does arithmetic on the numbers you type in — time, mileage, add-on fees, overhead, and margin — to suggest a price. It says nothing about what your state licence requires you to inspect, what your governing Standards of Practice cover, or what your errors-and-omissions policy actually insures. Verify all of that against your own licensing board and standards body.

Does anything I type get uploaded?

No. Every field on this page runs in your browser only, and nothing is sent to a server or an account. Your last job's numbers are saved locally on this device so you don't retype them. Usage counting only tallies anonymous feature events, and you can turn it off with the button above.

vs-a-flat-per-square-foot-rate.html.text:
← Home Inspection Fee Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat per-square-foot rate

A flat per-square-foot rate is easy to quote and easy to compare against another inspector's number — and it prices a 2,000 sqft one-story slab home built five years ago the same as a 2,000 sqft three-story crawlspace home built 60 years ago. This free calculator prices from stories, foundation type, and home age too, not square footage alone.

What each one actually captures

A flat per-square-foot rate multiplies one number by the home's floor area and stops there. It is fast, and floor area does set a real floor on how much there is to document — but it treats every home of the same size as the same job, whatever its stories, foundation, or age.

This calculator starts from square footage and adds the three specifics that actually drive on-site time at the same floor area: extra hours for each additional story climbed and inspected, extra hours for a crawlspace or basement foundation over a slab, and extra hours for an older home's likely deferred maintenance. Radon, sewer scope, termite/WDO, and mold add-ons are then priced at their own flat fee rather than folded into that time estimate, and a same-day rush premium applies to labor time only.

Run the same 2,000 square feet through both jobs this calculator's own defaults describe: a one-story slab home built five years ago estimates at 2.5 on-site hours and a $398.67 fee. A three-story crawlspace home built 60 years ago — same 2,000 square feet — estimates at 4.5 on-site hours and a $665.33 fee. A flat per-square-foot rate charges both the same; the actual on-site time differs by 80%. See a full worked example for how the numbers move line by line.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What's a fast, comparable number to quote off the bat?A flat per-square-foot rate — and this calculator's suggested fee is just as fast to get to.
Does the price account for stories, foundation type, and age at the same square footage?This calculator does. A flat per-square-foot rate cannot, by construction.
Two homes are the same size but one has a crawlspace and three stories — should they cost the same?Not on this calculator's model — see the 2.5 vs. 4.5-hour example above.
How do I price radon, sewer scope, termite/WDO, or mold add-ons?This calculator's add-on fields — priced as flat fees, not folded into the per-square-foot number.
Am I booking enough jobs to hit a weekly income target?This calculator's weekly income check, from your own profit-per-job and booking count.
Is my data uploaded anywhere?No, either way — a flat rate needs no tool at all, and this calculator keeps every number on your own device.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and nothing you type is uploaded anywhere.

Common questions

Isn't square footage the simplest way to price an inspection?

It's the simplest number to start from, and it does set a real floor on inspection time — more floor area is more area to document either way. The problem is stopping there. Two homes of identical square footage can take very different amounts of on-site time depending on stories, foundation type, and age, and a single per-square-foot rate has no way to tell them apart.

What does a flat per-square-foot rate miss?

Three specifics that actually drive on-site time at the same floor area: stories (climbing and inspecting an additional level), foundation type (a crawlspace means suiting up and physically moving through a tight space a slab does not require), and home age (an older home usually has more deferred maintenance to document). A flat rate folds all three into one number, which quietly underprices the harder combination and overprices the easier one.

How much can two same-size homes actually differ in on-site time?

Using this calculator's own default hourly rate and job costs: a 2,000 square foot one-story home on a slab, built five years ago, runs an estimated 2.5 on-site hours and prices at $398.67. A 2,000 square foot three-story home on a crawlspace, built 60 years ago — same floor area — runs an estimated 4.5 hours and prices at $665.33. A flat per-square-foot rate charges both the same; the actual on-site time differs by 80%.

Is this calculator affiliated with any pricing guide, rate service, or franchise?

No. This page compares against pricing purely by a flat per-square-foot rate — a generic estimating shortcut, not any specific guide, rate service, or franchise brand — so it names none. It is a separate question from this venture's own comparison against a franchise's internal fee schedule, which is about the business decision of joining a franchise, not about which pricing method to use.

Open the Home Inspection Fee Calculator to price your own job, read a full worked example, or see how this compares to a franchise's fee schedule if you're weighing that decision too.

vs-franchise-fee-schedule.html.text:
← Home Inspection Fee Calculator

This calculator vs. a franchise's internal fee schedule

Different situations. A home inspection franchise hands its inspectors a fee schedule already built for the brand. An independent inspector has to build their own — and pricing purely by square footage quietly underprices a hard job and overprices an easy one. This free calculator prices from the specifics that actually drive on-site time.

What each one is for

A franchise's internal fee schedule comes bundled with joining that franchise — brand recognition, referral pipelines, training, and often software, alongside a royalty or fee structure. That is a business decision about the inspector's whole operation, not just one job's price, and it is not what this page is about.

This calculator answers the narrower question an independent inspector already faces without a franchise's schedule behind them: what should this specific job cost. It prices from square footage, stories, foundation type, and home age — the factors that actually drive on-site time — rather than square footage alone, then adds radon, sewer scope, termite/WDO, and mold testing as their own flat fees and a same-day rush premium applied to labor time only. It needs no account, no brand affiliation, and nothing uploaded.

It exists because a flat per-square-foot number prices an easy slab job and a hard crawlspace job the same, which overcharges one buyer and undercharges the inspector on the other. See a full worked example for exactly how the numbers move.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What should I charge for this specific job, right now?This calculator's suggested fee — free, private, no account.
Does my fee schedule already account for stories, foundation, and age?Check against this calculator's model if you're not sure it does.
Should I join a franchise for its brand, referrals, and fee schedule?A business decision this calculator does not evaluate.
How do I price radon, sewer scope, termite/WDO, or mold add-ons?This calculator's add-on fields — priced as flat fees, not folded into time.
Am I booking enough jobs to hit a weekly income target?This calculator's weekly income check, from your own profit-per-job and booking count.
Is my data uploaded anywhere?No. Everything runs in your browser; your last job's numbers stay on this device.

This calculator is a general-purpose model, not a reproduction of any specific franchise's proprietary numbers, and it does not evaluate whether joining one is a good business decision. It is arithmetic on numbers you provide, not licensing, insurance, or business advice.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and nothing you type is uploaded anywhere.

Common questions

Should an independent inspector use this calculator or join a franchise for its fee schedule?

Different decisions. Joining a franchise brings a built-in fee schedule along with brand recognition, referral pipelines, training, and a royalty or fee structure — a business decision well beyond pricing one job. This calculator answers the narrower question an independent already faces without a franchise behind them: what should this specific job cost, given its square footage, stories, foundation type, and age. It does not evaluate whether joining a franchise makes sense.

Why does pricing purely by square footage underprice some jobs and overprice others?

Because square footage alone does not capture what actually drives on-site time. A crawlspace foundation means suiting up and physically moving through a tight space that a slab or basement does not require; an older home usually has more deferred maintenance to document at the same square footage as a newer one; an additional story adds real minutes to climb and inspect. Two houses of identical square footage can take very different amounts of time, so a single per-square-foot number prices the easy job and the hard job the same — overcharging one buyer and undercharging the inspector on the other.

Does this calculator replace a franchise's own fee schedule?

No, and it is not built to. A franchise's internal fee schedule is proprietary to that brand and may reflect brand-specific factors this calculator has no visibility into. This calculator is a general-purpose model built from the factors that drive on-site time for any inspector, independent or franchised, and it does not claim to reproduce any specific brand's numbers.

Can add-on services like radon or sewer scope testing be priced the same way as the base inspection?

Not usually, which is why this calculator prices them separately. A radon test, sewer scope, termite/WDO inspection, or mold air sample is typically a separate instrument or specialist step rather than additional minutes of the same walk-through, so each is priced as its own flat fee rather than folded into the time-based base estimate.
